title: The Common Feedback That You Don’t Bring People Along With You
author: Admired Leadership Field Notes
summary: The feedback is one of the most common pieces of 360-review language a fast-moving leader receives, and the authors make the useful move of splitting it in two. There are actually two distinct problems hiding inside "you don't bring people along." The first is communicating the rationale behind the leader's thinking and task requests. The second is gaining subscription to the resulting plan, usually through inclusion in the work of shaping it. The piece focuses on the first because subscription has been covered in earlier Field Notes, and because the communication failure is the one that most often catches high-capacity leaders by surprise. The diagnostic is sharp. Facile leaders who, like sharks, are in constant motion tend to run several steps ahead of the team before anyone else has seen the problem. That speed is a genuine strength until the leader fails to stop and say what they are seeing, what strategy they are forming, and what reasoning underlies the requests being handed down. Team members asked to execute on conclusions they do not understand either execute without rigor or intentionally drag their feet because the absence of explanation reads as disrespect. Over time, uncertainty becomes disengagement and rigor drops out of the work. The corrective is two-part and deceptively simple. Tell the team what you are seeing, what you are thinking, and why, before any plan takes shape. Then invite them to probe the evidence and the reasoning rather than debate the conclusions. The move is not to surrender the decision, it is to open the working assumptions to challenge from the people who will have to execute against them. Good leaders bring people along by making their reasoning audible and inspectable, which is the work that closes the gap between a fast leader and a team that can actually keep pace.
points: The central argument of this piece is grounded in the author's engagement with how real people think and act, not in idealized or abstract reasoning.
The takeaway is actionable,it can be implemented at the classroom or school level without waiting for policy change or external resources.
The piece challenges a common default assumption in education practice and offers a concrete alternative framed by evidence or lived experience.
The stakes are clear: what happens if leaders or teachers adopt this approach, and what is the cost of continuing the current default.
quotes: As it turns out, the problem of bringing people along can refer to two different issues: communicating the rationale for the leader’s thinking and task requests, and gaining buy-in to the strategy or plan (usually through inclusion).

The first step in bringing people along is for leaders to explain what they are seeing, what strategy and actions they are contemplating, and what the reasoning or rationale is underlying the requests they make of others before the plan takes any shape or form.

Facile leaders and those who, like sharks, are in constant movement, often think five steps ahead of any problem, issue, or opportunity. This is an unusual strength—unless the leader doesn’t take the time or make the effort to tell the team what they are seeing and thinking.

When the team doesn’t understand the rationale behind the leader’s directions that spring from this thinking, they don’t execute their part with rigor or vigor. In some cases, team members will intentionally resist directions or tasks set unilaterally without explanation, no matter how smart they believe the leader to be. They resist because they weren’t informed, which they interpret as a sign of disrespect.

Team members who work with leaders who fail to bring them along with their reasoning are often tasked to address problems or opportunities they don’t fully understand, which severely dilutes their effectiveness. Without understanding the consequences or implications of the problem, they often become confused when new tasks are assigned.

Good leaders not only take the time and make the effort to include the team with what they are thinking and seeing, they also ask them to probe their logic and evidence. They don’t debate with the team about the conclusions they are forming. Instead, they ask them to examine the reasoning and evidence underlying those conclusions.
In other words, they not only explain the problem or opportunity set but also ask for the team’s help in challenging their working assumptions.

Including people in what they are thinking, contemplating, seeing, and concluding is what good leaders do to bring people along. It is well worth the effort. Without it, teams flounder with uncertainty and weak execution.” Archived from Admired Leadership on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
